title: How 3 business owners raised prices in 2026 without losing customers
summary: Raise your prices without fear: Learn from three founders who raised their prices and kept their businesses growing without alienating their customers.
body_markdown:
Every founder has to do it eventually, but it can feel like one of the most nerve-wracking parts of running a business:


Raising your prices.


Imposter syndrome can hit hard. *Will our customers leave to find a cheaper option? What if our work drops off and the business starts to sink? Maybe we’ll just wait six more months and see …*


But wait too long, and your business will be stuck and unable to grow. It’s a classic founder dilemma. And it’s delicate enough that the three business owners who showed us how they raised prices only agreed to talk on one condition: we keep their real names out of it.


##


Act 1: The impetus


The first thing to note: nothing was catastrophically *wrong* .


All of the founders we interviewed had successful businesses. But just because nothing’s *wrong* doesn’t mean your business is thriving as much as it could be. That’s the inflection point that many founders find themselves at, waffling between what *could* be and the fear of the unknown.


We talked to three founders*:


1. **Sally, co-owner of a home services business in a mid-sized city in North Carolina.** Things were going well until a general contractor told her she was bidding ~75% under market. They undercharged to stay competitive and get their foot in the door with big established names in the area. But over time, their rates were too low to sustainably cover their expenses.


2. **Peter, co-owner of a residential and office cleaning business in the LA area.** His partner had started as an independent cleaner, and they’d since grown into a full cleaning business. The problem was they were still charging $40 per hour in a $70–$75 per-hour market. After pricing out the cost of goods, labor, and expenses, he realized they weren’t competitive with other cleaning businesses.


Peter told us, “\[We\] had a ton of customers, were always busy, and employed a lot of people, but the[cleaning business itself just wasn’t very profitable](https://www.quo.com/blog/is-a-cleaning-business-profitable/) .”


1. **Ian, co-founder of a dermatology clinic in the Pacific Northwest.** Ian’s clinic was booking out further and further in advance. First it was 30 days, then 45, then 60 days booked out. After almost two years, he ran the numbers and realized his medical appointments earned less than half of what his aesthetic ones did per hour. Short of being able to make more hours in the day — wouldn’t that be nice? — he realized the only way to increase revenue was to raise prices.


The throughline: sometimes things seem to be going well, until you sit down and look at the hard data. Even if your prices are working okay *right now* , that doesn’t mean they’re sustainable long term.


**Names and some identifying details have been changed.*


##


Act 2: The fear


The thing that holds most founders back from raising prices isn’t data, business knowledge, or indecision. It’s usually fear.


*What if our clients leave for somewhere cheaper?*


*What if we’re shooting way above our level?*


*What if all our current demand drops off?*


Sally summed it up bluntly:


> “I was preparing myself to be rejected by our old customers.”


If you’re raising prices to stay competitive in-market or reflect your true value, new customers won’t question it. But legacy clients or[existing customers](https://www.quo.com/blog/customer-retention-management/) who are used to a lower price? How will they respond when you tell them they need to start paying more for the same services?


##


Act 3: Making the leap: How they‌ did it


Sometimes, the hardest part is ripping off the band-aid. The key is finding the right way to do it to bring your customers *along with you* rather than alienating them. Here’s how these business owners managed the leap:


### Give advance written notice


Ian and Sally both sent emails; Peter used the Quo API to text all his customers. No one did it by phone — which makes sense. Written notice is more official. It[puts things in writing](https://www.quo.com/blog/sms-compliance/) for a clear paper trail, and gives customers something they can refer back to. Plus, it’s easier to email or text your entire customer base than to call each customer individually.


Sally and Ian also both gave advance notice.


- Ian plans to implement new prices for existing customers in 2027. He emailed their existing patient base in September 2026. That way, patients don’t feel blindsided and have time to prepare.
- Sally raised prices at the beginning of the year. She sent an email heads-up a few months before the change. She sent one again at the beginning of the year, when the new prices went into effect.


Fun fact: Peter used the[Quo API](https://www.quo.com/api) to pull a list of 100+ existing customers and text them all individually within 5-10 minutes.[Here’s how you can do the same](https://www.quo.com/docs/mdx/api-reference/send-your-first-message?ps_partner_key=YzZiZGQ5ZTBlMDcy&ps_xid=Ce0lhPvdNIWECO#send-your-first-message) .


### Provide a clear justification


Be honest with your customers and give them a reason for the rate change. “We need to make more money” probably won’t go over well. But clients understand external, reasonable factors for the change.


Peter knew that they needed to raise prices right away, so he[texted their customers](https://www.quo.com/blog/sample-text-messages-to-customers/) to do a small rate increase effective immediately.


> “We sent out a message saying, ‘Hey, this is a price increase we need to do to support our cleaning team. It helps ensure that we can continue to provide the same level and quality of service. As the costs of doing business rise, we need to do a small price increase as well to provide you with high-quality service.’”


Sally also cited rising costs in her email:


> “One of the main reasons we gave \[for the price increase\] was that the overhead costs of doing business were expanding. The economy had also just taken a huge dive, and gas was skyrocketing. So I also mentioned that the cost of fuel for traveling to everyone was pretty high. We service a big geographic area, \[so gas is a big factor\].”


You don’t have to get into the nitty-gritty or share your expense balances. But providing a clear, external justification helps customers feel more at ease with the changes.


### Start small to reduce risk


You don’t have to overhaul your pricing overnight. All of these business owners found a low-risk way to start. This not only helps ease your own fears, but it also confirms your new prices can compete in the marketplace. Here’s how they did it:


- Ian started by first raising prices with new patients. In a second phase, they’ll raise prices for existing patients by 25%.
- Peter started by raising prices from $40 an hour to $45 an hour. He plans to raise prices further to better align with market rates but started with a small increase across the board.
- Sally started by raising prices for all new customers and then raising rates for existing customers. Existing customers went from paying $45–$55 every two weeks to $65–$75, depending on the service, a 35%-45% increase.


### Anticipate pushback


Peter and Sally both anticipated and addressed pushback from the start. One way they did so was by reinforcing their positioning and messaging to back up their new prices.


Instead of competing based on price, they adopted and strengthened their positioning as a more premium service. For example, Peter specifically named their 24-hour cleaning service guarantee. He noted that the price increase helped them continue to deliver and offer this guarantee.


Sally used a similar positioning:


> “I’ve always had the belief that if you’re going to pay to have something done, it should be done correctly. A lot of \[competitor\] services in the area provide the bare minimum, and you get “okay” service. I wanted our prices to be fair but still give great quality work.”


Peter also responded to pushback by anchoring his new pricing against competitors:


> “We tried to communicate that our prices are still really competitive in the market. We provided \[some clients\] with the names of a few of our competitors. We said, ’\[competitor\] or \[competitor\] would charge you $75 an hour,’ showing that we’re still very competitive in terms of rates, and we offer the same things they offer.”


Bottom line: if you’re no longer competing on price, own it. It’s okay if you’re not the cheapest option, as long as you give clients a reason to keep working with you.


##


Act 4: The reaction


You hit send on the email and hold your breath. How are customers going to react? According to the business owners we talked to, the big reaction was mostly nothing.


Ian raised prices and waited for a drop in demand, but‌ “nothing really happened,” he said.


> “We haven’t detected much of a change in demand or conversion at all.”


Of Sally’s existing client base, just three left after they raised their prices. Of those, one came back, saying, “Yeah… you guys still do it way better, even though you’re more expensive” — a confirmation of her premium positioning.


> “I was very surprised, because I went through \[our list\] and thought, ‘Oh, this person’s going to leave. This person’s going to leave. This person’s going to leave.’ And actually, the people I thought were going to leave didn’t even flinch, didn’t even question it.”


Peter had a similar experience. After messaging his entire existing customer base that prices were going up immediately, he told us,


> “There were a handful of people who were not happy with it, but the overwhelming majority didn’t care. \[Of the people who weren’t happy,\] I think as long as we gave people an understandable reason, I would say half of those people were then, ‘Okay, yeah, sounds good.’ We ended up losing like 2-3 customers max out of \[around\] 100 people that we messaged.”


Their fears were mostly unfounded. Demand didn’t drop out. Their business didn’t fall apart. Most of their existing customers didn’t even flinch.


This isn’t luck or a one-off experience. Customers know that prices go up over time, and the right customers are willing to pay for services they can trust. As Peter said, “The people who are viewing us as a budget cleaning service are maybe not the customers that we want to keep in the long term.”


##


Act 5: The new routine


Once you know your prices can move and[grow with your business](https://www.quo.com/blog/lead-management/) , underpricing yourself becomes an obvious mistake.


All of these founders have no regrets.


As Ian said, “\[It was\] the right approach to increase our price for new patients once we were full, which represented the only way to raise revenue per hour once we were fully booked.” Even with a fully booked calendar, there’s room for growth. Start with raising the rates for new clients, then follow Ian’s lead and schedule a small bump for existing clients 3-6 months out.


Sally was surprised that some of her clients weren’t just okay with the change, they’d‌ been expecting it. She told us, “One client even said, ‘I was expecting you to raise your prices a couple of months ago. You’ve been doing this for me for two years now.”


This reaction reconfirmed that clients know and expect price increases as the cost of doing business grows. But aside from that, Sally said,


> “I feel like \[raising our prices\] made us more stable. We still have those prices now, and we have also been able to add more services to what we already had, and we’ve not \[yet\] had to raise prices on any of them. So I feel like it’s made us more stable overall.”


If you’re looking to raise your prices — now or more regularly — Sally said, “Just do your research. It took me six to eight months to even get up the gumption to raise my prices and send the first email because I was so scared. So I did research for months to figure out what the \[fair market price\] would be, what my baseline was going to be moving forward, and what I could afford to lose if I had to. Sometimes you need to figure out what you’re willing to lose to see what you can gain.”
